![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081888/assets/8b7b81c97a842b82c2e4cbbd041883c1bd7f4f4ab58dc6592c12ec1cc0262620.png)

Which integral expression gives the total area enclosed between the curve $y={x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above?
worked_solution:
First, we find the limits of integration. We find the $x$-intercepts of the curve as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-2x-3) & =0 \\ x(x+1)(x-3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $x=-1,x=0$ or $x=3.$ Since $0\in [-1,3],$ we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=0.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=3.$

For $x\in [-1,0]$, we have

$$
{A}_{1}={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that for $x\in [0,3]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
{A}_{2}=-{\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{3}-({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{3}-({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$
